ELECTIVE AREA · JUNE · JULY

How people learned to count and calculate

Notches in a bone, wedges in damp clay, hieroglyphs on stone, Roman numerals on clocks and counters on lines: before there were our digits, people found many ways of recording numbers. In this elective area you read and write the numerals of different times and cultures, calculate like Adam Ries and put together a presentation.

8 LESSONS4 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • how people counted without digits: tally charts, tally sticks, counting with the body
  • read and write the numerals of the Babylonians, Egyptians and Romans
  • convert numbers from these systems into the decimal system and back
  • add and subtract with counters on the lines
  • put together a presentation about a number system
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

How many minutes does an hour have?

60 minutes. You will meet the number 60 again in this chapter.

Which number has 3 tens and 4 ones?

$3 \times 10 + 4 = 34$

How many fingers do two hands have?

10. Perhaps that is the reason for our decimal system.

Calculate: $2 \times 60 + 5$

$120 + 5 = 125$

UNIT 12 LESSONS

1Counting with strokes and notches

Before there were digits, people remembered amounts with strokes, with notches in wood or bone, with pebbles or with knots in strings. One mark for every thing counted: that is the simplest way of recording a number.

With lots of strokes you soon lose track. That is why you bundle them: in a tally chart you always group five strokes together, four upright and the fifth across them. On a tally stick, debts, for example, were cut in as notches; often every fifth or tenth notch was longer.

But for people, numbers were not only there for counting. Some were thought of as lucky or unlucky numbers, such as 7 or 13. In China 8 is a lucky number, because its name sounds similar to the word for wealth.

KEY POINT · BUNDLING

One stroke or notch for every thing. Bundling makes counting easier: in a tally chart five strokes are always grouped together.

Number systems begin with bundling: our decimal system always bundles ten, the Babylonians bundled into tens and sixties.

A saying: in German, someone who “has something on the tally stick” has done something wrong; the debts used to be written there. In England the Treasury kept its accounts on tally sticks until 1826.

Counting with the body: the Oksapmin in Papua New Guinea count along 27 places on the body. For them the nose is 14.

INTERACTIVE · TALLY STICK AND TALLY CHART

Add notches. At the top is the tally stick, below it the same number as a tally chart with bundles of five.

EXAMPLE 1 · READING A TALLY CHART

A tally chart has three bundles of five and two single strokes. How many strokes is that?

Three bundles of 5 each and another 2: $3 \times 5 + 2$.

17 strokes

EXAMPLE 2 · COUNTING ON THE BODY

For the Oksapmin the thumb is 1 and the nose is 14. On the other side of the body the count goes back down to the other little finger. Which number is it?

Up to the nose there are 14 places. On the other side come the same 13 places as on the way there, only backwards: $14 + 13 = 27$.

The little finger of the other hand is 27.

EXERCISES

Make a tally chart: how do the pupils in your class get to school, on foot, by bike, by bus or by car?

One stroke in the right row for each answer, every fifth one across. At the end you count the bundles and the single strokes.

How many strokes are 4 bundles of five and 3 single strokes?

$4 \times 5 + 3 = 23$

Why do you bundle exactly five strokes in a tally chart? What would be worse about bundles of ten strokes?

You can recognise five strokes at a glance without counting, like the fingers of one hand. Ten strokes side by side you already have to count one by one.

There are 37 notches on a tally stick. Every tenth notch is longer. How many long notches are there?

The long notches are the 10th, 20th and 30th: three of them.

A tally stick for debts was often split along its length: whoever owed money got one half, whoever had lent it got the other. Why could nobody cheat like this?

The notches went across both halves. If you put the halves back together, all the notches must match up exactly. A notch secretly added or cut away would be seen at once.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many strokes are 6 bundles of five?

$6 \times 5 = 30$

How many bundles of five do you need for 45 strokes?

$45 \div 5 = 9$

How many single strokes are left over from 23 strokes if you make bundles of five?

$23 = 4 \times 5 + 3$: three single strokes.

UNIT 22 LESSONS

2Babylonians and Egyptians

About 4,000 years ago scribes in Mesopotamia, today’s Iraq, pressed wedge-shaped marks into soft clay with a stylus: cuneiform. For numbers the Babylonians needed only two symbols: an upright wedge for 1 and a corner wedge for 10.

Up to 59, wedges and corner wedges are simply written next to each other. At 60 a new place begins further to the left, worth 60 times as much, and after that one worth 3,600 times as much. That is a base-60 system with place values, rather like our decimal system.

The Egyptians wrote numbers with hieroglyphs: a stroke for 1, a hobble for 10, a coil of rope for 100 and a lotus flower for 1,000. Each symbol is written as often as it is needed. Where it stands does not matter, and you do not need a zero.

KEY POINT · BABYLONIAN AND EGYPTIAN

Babylonians: wedge = 1, corner wedge = 10. Place values 1, 60, 3,600, … from right to left: $2{,}026 = 33 \times 60 + 46$.

Egyptians: stroke 1, hobble 10, coil of rope 100, lotus 1,000. No place value: the symbols are simply added up.

60 lives on: 1 h = 60 min, 1 min = 60 s, and a full turn has $6 \times 60 = 360$ degrees.

Without zero: for a long time the Babylonians had no symbol for an empty place. A 1 and a 60 looked the same; you had to guess from the context.

INTERACTIVE · CUNEIFORM

Set a number, for example the year you were born. With “+ 60” you can see how the second place grows.

INTERACTIVE · HIEROGLYPHS

The same number in Egyptian numerals. Switch to the Romans as well.

EXAMPLE 3 · WRITING IN BABYLONIAN

How does a Babylonian scribe write the number 75?

$75 = 1 \times 60 + 15$. On the left a place with 1 wedge, on the right a place with 1 corner wedge and 5 wedges.

1 wedge  |  1 corner wedge and 5 wedges

EXAMPLE 4 · WRITING IN EGYPTIAN

How many symbols does an Egyptian scribe need for 2,345?

2 lotus flowers, 3 coils of rope, 4 hobbles and 5 strokes: $2 + 3 + 4 + 5$.

14 symbols

EXERCISES

Describe how the Babylonians wrote: a) 23   b) 59   c) 61   d) 130

a) 2 corner wedges, 3 wedges   b) 5 corner wedges, 9 wedges   c) 1 wedge | 1 wedge, because $61 = 1 \times 60 + 1$   d) 2 wedges | 1 corner wedge, because $130 = 2 \times 60 + 10$

How many Egyptian symbols do you need for 999? And for 1,000?

For 999: $9 + 9 + 9 = 27$ symbols. For 1,000: a single lotus flower.

A Babylonian number: on the left 3 corner wedges and 3 wedges, on the right 4 corner wedges and 6 wedges. Which number is it?

On the left 33, on the right 46: $33 \times 60 + 46 = 1{,}980 + 46 = 2{,}026$. This number is also on the cover of the book.

How many minutes and seconds are 200 seconds? What does that have to do with the Babylonians?

$200 = 3 \times 60 + 20$, so 3 min 20 s. That is exactly how a Babylonian would write 200: 3 wedges | 2 corner wedges. Our clock time still works in base 60 today.

How many Egyptian symbols do you need for 9,999? Compare with our digits. What is the advantage of a place value system?

$9 + 9 + 9 + 9 = 36$ symbols; we only need 4 digits. In a place value system the place says how much a digit is worth, so a few symbols are enough even for huge numbers.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is a wedge in the second place from the right worth for the Babylonians?

60

Babylonian: on the left 1 wedge, on the right 3 corner wedges. Which number is it?

$1 \times 60 + 30 = 90$

How many Egyptian symbols do you need for 1,111?

One symbol each for 1,000, 100, 10 and 1: four symbols.

UNIT 32 LESSONS

3Roman numerals

You can still see them today on clocks, on old buildings and in the credits of films: Roman numerals. MMXXVI means 2026.

The Romans used letters as numerals. Usually the values are simply added: XVII is $10 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 17$. So that numbers do not get too long, there is a second rule: if a smaller symbol stands in front of a bigger one, it is subtracted. IV is $5 - 1 = 4$, XC is $100 - 10 = 90$.

Calculating with Roman numerals is hard work. When adding, you push the symbols together and bundle them: IIIII becomes V, VV becomes X. Multiplying is almost impossible, because there is no place value and no zero.

KEY POINT · ROMAN NUMERALS

I = 1  ·  V = 5  ·  X = 10  ·  L = 50  ·  C = 100  ·  D = 500  ·  M = 1,000

The values are added. If a smaller symbol stands in front of a bigger one, it is subtracted: IV = 4, IX = 9, XL = 40, XC = 90, CD = 400, CM = 900. The same symbol appears at most three times in a row.

Clocks: many clock faces show IIII instead of IV.

Only subtract like this: I in front of V and X, X in front of L and C, C in front of D and M. 99 is XCIX, not IC.

INTERACTIVE · ROMAN NUMERALS

Set a number and read it in Roman numerals. Below the picture you can see which symbols are added and which are subtracted.

EXAMPLE 5 · READING

Which year is MCMLXXXIV?

M = 1,000, CM = 900, L = 50, XXX = 30, IV = 4.

$1{,}000 + 900 + 50 + 30 + 4 = 1{,}984$

EXAMPLE 6 · ADDING THE ROMAN WAY

Add XXVII and XVI without converting into our digits.

Push them together: XXX, VV, III. Bundle: VV becomes X, so XXXX and III. Shorter: XXXX is XL.

XXVII + XVI = XLIII, so $27 + 16 = 43$

EXERCISES

Write with our digits: XIV, XXXIX, LXXV, CDXLIV, MMXXVI

14, 39, 75, 444, 2026

Write in Roman numerals: 8, 19, 49, 90, 1,500 and the year you were born.

VIII, XIX, XLIX, XC, MD. For example 2015 = MMXV, 2016 = MMXVI.

Add the Roman way, without converting: XXXV + XXVI

Together: XXXXX, VV, I. Bundle: XXXXX becomes L, VV becomes X. Result LXI, so $35 + 26 = 61$.

Above a school gate it says MDCCCLXXII. In which year was the school built?

$1{,}000 + 500 + 300 + 50 + 20 + 2 = 1{,}872$. Since that same year the metre has applied throughout Germany.

Try to work out XV × XXIII without converting into our digits. Why is it such hard work?

Every symbol of one number has to be multiplied by every symbol of the other.

X × XXIII = CCXXX and V × XXIII = CXV, together CCCXLV = 345. Without place value you have to deal with every symbol separately and bundle a lot at the end. With our digits it is much quicker in columns.

TEST YOURSELF!

Which number is XLII?

XL = 40, II = 2: 42

Which number is MCM?

M = 1,000, CM = 900: 1,900

How many symbols does 38 have in Roman numerals?

XXXVIII: seven symbols.

UNIT 42 LESSONS

4Calculating on the lines and a presentation

500 years ago merchants in Germany did not yet calculate in writing with digits. They put counters on a counting board with lines. Adam Ries, who lived in Annaberg in the Ore Mountains, wrote arithmetic books about it, from which many people learned to calculate.

On the counting board there are horizontal lines for 1, 10, 100 and 1,000. The spaces above them count 5, 50 and 500. There are at most four counters on a line and at most one in a space. If there are more, they are bundled.

To add, you put the counters of the second number with them and bundle from the bottom upwards. To subtract, you take counters away. If there are not enough, you exchange one counter on the line above for smaller ones.

KEY POINT · CALCULATING ON THE LINES

Lines: 1, 10, 100, 1,000  ·  spaces: 5, 50, 500

Bundling: 5 counters on a line become 1 counter in the space above. 2 counters in a space become 1 counter on the line above.

Adam Ries (about 1492 to 1559): in Germany people still say “that makes, according to Adam Ries, …” when a calculation is right.

Presentation: one slide or poster for each number system: the symbols, an example, an advantage, a disadvantage, a source.

INTERACTIVE · THE COUNTING BOARD

Two numbers are laid out on the lines and added. Follow step by step how they are bundled.

EXAMPLE 7 · LAYING OUT A NUMBER

How do you lay out 37 on the lines?

30: 3 counters on the tens line. 7 = 5 + 2: 1 counter in the space above the ones line and 2 on the ones line.

3 + 1 + 2 = 6 counters

EXAMPLE 8 · PLANNING A PRESENTATION

Your group is presenting Roman numerals. How can you structure the presentation?

1. Where do the symbols come from? 2. The seven symbols and the rules. 3. An example, such as the year you were born. 4. A calculation. 5. An advantage and a disadvantage. 6. Where you got your information from.

Little text, big symbols, an example to join in with.

EXERCISES

Describe how you lay out these numbers on the lines: 8, 26, 359, 1,204.

8: 1 in the fives space, 3 on the ones line. 26: 2 on the tens line, 1 in the fives space, 1 on the ones line. 359: 3 on the hundreds line, 1 in the fifties space, 1 in the fives space, 4 on the ones line. 1,204: 1 on the thousands line, 2 on the hundreds line, 4 on the ones line.

Add $748 + 386$ on the lines and describe where you have to bundle.

Result 1,134. You bundle the ones (14 → 1 ten and 4), the tens (13 → 1 hundred and 3) and the hundreds (11 → 1 thousand and 1).

With your group, plan a presentation about a number system from this chapter. Write down what goes on each slide or each part of the poster.

For example: title, origin and time, the symbols, an example, calculating with it, advantages and disadvantages, sources. Each person takes on one part.

Invent a number system of your own with symbols for 1, 6 and 36. Use it to write 50 and 100.

For example ● = 1, ▲ = 6, ■ = 36. $50 = 36 + 6 + 6 + 1 + 1$: ■ ▲ ▲ ● ●. $100 = 2 \times 36 + 4 \times 6 + 4 \times 1$: ■ ■ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ● ● ● ●.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is a counter in the space between the tens line and the hundreds line worth?

50

How many counters are on the counting board for the number 9?

$9 = 5 + 4$: 1 counter in the space and 4 on the ones line, 5 altogether.

How many counters are on the counting board for 2,026?

2 on the thousands line, 2 on the tens line, 1 in the fives space and 1 on the ones line: 6 counters.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

2026 three times: Write the number 2026 in Babylonian, Egyptian and Roman numerals.

Babylonian: 3 corner wedges and 3 wedges | 4 corner wedges and 6 wedges. Egyptian: 2 lotus flowers, 2 hobbles, 6 strokes. Roman: MMXXVI.

Counting symbols: How many symbols do you need for 888 in Egyptian, in Roman numerals and with our digits?

Egyptian $8 + 8 + 8 = 24$, Roman DCCCLXXXVIII with 12 symbols, our digits 3.

The clock: How many seconds are 2 h 15 min 30 s?

$2 \times 3{,}600 + 15 \times 60 + 30 = 7{,}200 + 900 + 30 = 8{,}130$ s. Just like the place values of the Babylonians: 1, 60, 3,600.

To finish: Give three advantages of our decimal system with zero over the other numerals in this chapter.

For example: you only need ten symbols. Even large numbers are short. Zero keeps empty places free. You can calculate in columns, place by place.

EXCURSIONARCHAEOLOGY

The Ishango bone

In 1950 the Belgian researcher Jean de Heinzelin found a bone about 10 cm long with many notches at Ishango on Lake Edward, in what is today the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is about 20,000 years old; the experts are still arguing about its exact age. Today it is kept in the Museum of Natural Sciences in Brussels.

The 168 notches are arranged in three rows. In one row there are groups of 11, 13, 17 and 19 notches, exactly the prime numbers between 10 and 20. In another row there are 11, 21, 19 and 9 notches. Whether people were already calculating then, whether the bone was a calendar or whether it is all chance, nobody knows.

Try it yourself: Add up the notches in the two rows. In the third row there are the groups 3, 6, 4, 8, 10, 5, 5 and 7. What do you notice about 3 and 6, about 4 and 8 and about 10 and 5?

$11 + 13 + 17 + 19 = 60$ and $11 + 21 + 19 + 9 = 60$: 60 twice. The third row makes 48. The 3 is followed by its double, 6, the 4 by its double, 8, the 10 by its half, 5. Perhaps somebody was doubling and halving here.

Sources: Jean de Heinzelin, “Ishango”, Scientific American 206 (6), June 1962, pp. 105–116. Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, Brussels (ishango.naturalsciences.be).
